quietus.title: Quiet Storm by Space Afrika
quietus.description: Manchester duo go big, vastly expanding their palette with strings, harps and a plethora of special guests Photograph credit: Timon Benson. Art Direction: Alexander Luc and Timon Benson. Clothing: Omar Afridi X VUJA DÉ There is a particular kind of light that only exists after rain has finished falling but before the sun has arrived – a grey-gold hour where the wet ground holds more colour than the sky. Space Afrika has always made records that live inside that hour. Honest Labour, the pair's breakout 2021 statement, was full of it: shortwave murmur, tower-block wind, the feeling of being simultaneously inside a crowd and entirely alone. Five years on, Joshua Tarelle Reid and Joshua Inyang…

quietus.title: Immersion – What Is Lost Will Return
quietus.description: Immersion What Is Lost Will Return Immersion find new shapes within familiar sounds, turning repetition into something restless What Is Lost Will Return by Immersion Given the history behind Immersion, it would be easy to hear What Is Lost Will Return as a record looking backwards. That is a useful quality for a band with Colin Newman and Malka Spigel’s respective histories: there is no shortage of past to draw upon. But What Is Lost Will Return feels pleasingly unconcerned with doing so. It occupies a strange, immediate space somewhere between song, groove and electronic abstraction, where guitars, bass, electronics and voices seem to be continually finding new combinations. ‘Nephology’…

Comprised of four long-form tracks, the project came about from conversations that the two artists, on opposite sides of the world, had in 2021 about the volatile environments that they found themselves in, as Australia experience flooding and extreme weather, and Ireland's Atlantic coastline was hit by storms. In a joint statement, Skeleton and English said: “NOON operates as a palindrome of listening practices and experimentation, and moreover as a shared temporal marker that reminds us of the vastly finite turnings of our world." Watch a…

It marks the first release of new music from the artist since last year's album…

Plus, 10 crucial new records, from Spanish electroclash bagpipes to Millinerian weirdness from Leeds Sara Parkman performs live at the inaugural Supertraditional Festival. Photo by Isak Gudnason Before we begin, I can't recommend enough that any England-based readers catch La Tène and Sourdure, two outliers of the French radical folk scene, at their forthcoming Cafe OTO show this Saturday (26 September). I reviewed La Tène live in my last column, and I stand by every…

quietus.title: Merryn Jeann – Fear Of The Beauty Parlour
quietus.description: Merryn Jeann Fear Of The Beauty Parlour Australian singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist finds tenderness in fragments on her second album At what point does a song stop being a song? Strip away the beat, harmony and narrative; leave behind a voice, a melody, a few repeated words, the hiss of a phone recording. Merryn Jeann’s Fear Of The Beauty Parlour seems fascinated by precisely that threshold. Jeann has never been particularly interested in conventional singer-songwriting. In the Australian artist’s music, the voice can transform into an instrument, a simple melody can suddenly break off, and an intimate story can give way to a field recording, a strange synth sound or a…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Love :: Four Sail
aquariumdrunkard.description: For many, Forever Changes is where the Love story ends. Whether viewed as a retooled evolution of the band or simply that of Arthur Lee, Four Sail is an essential part of the Love discography. With a driving edge partly recalling the proto-punk energy of Da Capo with the modern hard rock zeitgeist of 1969, Lee's superb new lineup delivers the intentions behind "combining the east and west coast sounds with the European sounds, plus a few of my own ideas".

aquariumdrunkard.title: Transmissions :: Matt Baldwin
aquariumdrunkard.description: This week on the show, guitarist and psychotherapist Matt Baldwin, who is here to teach you How To Play Guitar. OK, not exactly. But Baldwin is the author of ⁠How To Play Guitar⁠, a series of zines that have been collected into a handsome book edition. If you’re just picking up the instrument, well, Baldwin isn’t writing about how to play a C chord or run scales. These aren’t “how to” guides so much as “why to” prompts, stressing intuition over technique, dismissal of music industry norms, and the imperative to hone a singular, personal philosophy regarding the instrument—think Captain Beefheart’s “Ten Commandments of Playing Guitar.” In this talk, we discuss his own guitar journey, the…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts :: Second Song
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 80, Neil Young remains gloriously unfinished. Second Song , his latest with the Chrome Hearts, is a weathered, luminous meditation on memory, mortality, love, and the strange passage of time. With shimmering textures, warm harmonies, wandering tempos, and that unmistakably vulnerable voice, Young looks backward without quite letting go of the future. An elegiac, deeply human record from an artist still searching for the song.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Índio da Cuíca :: Zing Zing
aquariumdrunkard.description: At 70, Brazilian percussionist Índio da Cuíca reinvented himself as one of the country’s strangest musical voices. His cuíca—usually a squeaky rhythmic accent—is transformed into a melodic instrument of uncanny virtuosity, set against samba, capoeira, Afro-Brazilian spirituals and warped pop forms. On Zing Zing , that “avant-traditional” vision expands further, as cavaquinho, pandeiro, berimbau and bandolim collide with guitars, synths and samples. Samba music from some parallel universe.

aquariumdrunkard.title: HUG :: HUG
aquariumdrunkard.description: Hug is music for the small hours, when the world comes in and out of focus, a record that drifts through the mind’s open windows, carrying with it the sublime and resonant hush of a world at peace in its own unfolding. As warm and comforting as the name implies, Hug embraces you like an old friend, holding space for the warmth of the past, the uncertainty of the future, and the solace of the blossoming present.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Maddy Prior & June Tabor’s Silly Sisters at 50
aquariumdrunkard.description: Maddy Prior and June Tabor’s Silly Sisters is a magical hinge album, a meeting of two transcendent voices and a jolly band of British folk masters. Recorded in 1976 but somehow outside of time, its ancient songs, close harmonies, and loose, luminous performances summon something older than the British folk revival itself. Fifty years on, it remains a timeless gem hiding in plain sight: raw, sophisticated, mysterious, and still not quite given its due.

Bringing together business people from more than 30 countries with the stated aim of accelerating investment in the country which has been beset by trade conflicts with the United States, the event also galvanized a range of community groups with diverse objections to protest the summit, which then brought hundreds of police officers and vehicles to the area just north of the festival center. mubi.title: Toronto Dispatch: The War Against Memory
mubi.description: Life of Jorge Luis Borges (Mariano Llinás, 2026). Words mean things, but that meaning is always changing. Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. After years of algorithmic censorship, we now see words like “unalive” or “le$bean” replacing their antecedents even in conversation, even if only ironically. (As if to prove the point, the plot of the new film by Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence , manages to hinge on the issue of assisted suicide without ever uttering the s-word. It’s as if the film anticipates the language that will be…

mubi.title: The Action Scene | “The Raid” at 15
mubi.description: The Action Scene explores the form, history, and visceral power of action cinema through its set pieces. Clockwise from top-left: The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011), Merantau (Gareth Evans, 2009), The Raid 2 (Gareth Evans, 2014), The Raid (Gareth Evans, 2011). It needs virtually no introduction. Fifteen years after its world premiere in the Midnight Madness section of the 2011 Toronto International Film Festival, The Raid (2011) has so shaped the landscape of contemporary action cinema that it’s birthed its own prepositional descriptor: “like The Raid ” adorns sundry headlines to describe any action film featuring some combination of a single-location setting, gritty atmosphere, barbarous…

mubi.title: Defending the Elusive
mubi.description: Last Year in Marienbad (Alain Resnais, 1961). 1 Although it’s seldom acknowledged, one of the supreme pleasures of movies is the confusion and uncertainty often prompted by the beginning of a story, when we’re not yet fully tuned in to what’s going on. As in our sleeping dreams, a sense of infinite possibility stretches before us. That seemingly limitless vista soon disappoints once it is foreshortened into something real and recognizable, such as a place, an environment, a mood, a character, a theme, a genre, or a plot. Yet without these comfortable anchors, something that resembles prenatal bliss envelops our ignorance, and the fact that we can imagine almost anything makes the start of…

I say “watch” when the more accurate verb would be “experience,” at least going by the fest’s preferred vocabulary for what goes down on Lazzaretto Vecchio, an island a stone’s throw away from the Lido. Once used as a checkpoint for Holy Land pilgrims, and then—after the plague reached the lagoon in 1423—a leper colony, it is, in 2026 AD, now home to the virtual reality sidebar. The architecture has barely changed through the centuries. Dotting the high-ceilinged corridors that used to house the city’s moribund, festival guests can find various booths, each promising…
